title: Shouldering
summary: Use your own king as a barrier: push the enemy king off the path instead of running straight ahead.
part.between.title: Between king and pawn
part.between.summary: The king doesn't chase the pawn: it stands in the other king's path, one step ahead of it.
part.wall.title: The king as a wall
part.wall.summary: Walk beside the enemy king, file by file, until it is too far away to help.
part.away.title: Away from the pawn
part.away.summary: Sometimes the best king move steps away from the pawn you want to win.
part.race.title: Shouldering in a race
part.race.summary: When both sides have a passed pawn, a king that blocks the other is worth a whole tempo.
part.defend.title: Shouldering in defence
part.defend.summary: The defender pushes too: keeping the attacking king away from the pawn saves half a point.
part.summary.title: Summary
part.summary.summary: Three rules of shouldering and a game to practise.
step.t_stairs: White to move. The black king is far from the pawn, and so is the white king. If the black king reaches the f-pawn, it's a draw. Which king move stops that?
step.t_stairs.hint1: Trace the black king's shortest route to f2. Which squares does it need?
step.t_stairs.hint2: The route goes through c4, d3 and e2. Your king can stand in front of that route, not behind it.
step.stairs: Kb3! The white king doesn't run to the pawn, it runs into the black king's path. From b3 it takes away c4, and the black king has to step aside. Each time it steps, my king takes the same step, on the same file, two ranks lower. That is shouldering: my king pushes the other one like a basketball player with his shoulder, without touching, just by taking up the space.
step.stairsDraw: Now the same position with Black to move. With Kc4, for example, the black king gets in front: d3, e2, and the pawn falls. A single tempo decides who pushes whom. That's why the shoulder has to come at once, on the first move.
step.d_stairs: Watch the white king walk down the stairs next to the black one. Always on its file, always two ranks lower.
step.d_stairs.m1: Kb3. I shut c4, the black king's way in.
step.d_stairs.m2: The black king tries the c-file, one rank higher.
step.d_stairs.m3: Kc3. Same step, and now d4 is shut.
step.d_stairs.m5: Kd3. I shut e4 and e2. The black king is still outside.
step.d_stairs.m7: Ke3. My king has reached the pawn without ever letting the other one through.
step.d_stairs.m8: Kf5, and the black king is still on the wrong side.
step.d_stairs.m9: Kf3. The pawn is protected and my king stands in front of it. From here on it's the key-squares technique.
step.stairsMove: White to move and win. Same idea, now with the pawn on g2. Walk down the stairs with the black king.
step.stairsMove.hint: Stay on the black king's file, two ranks below it, shutting the square it would come through.
step.stairsMove.done: Right. Each of your moves shut the door of the moment, and the black king never reached the pawn.
step.t_wall: White to move. Both sides have an f-pawn. The black king is far away on b4, but it wants to come back to defend f7. How do you keep it away?
step.t_wall.hint1: The black king has to cross the board to reach the kingside. Which file would it cross?
step.t_wall.hint2: A whole file can become a wall if your king walks along it, always level with the black king.
step.wall: Kd4! My king stops on the d-file and becomes a wall: c3, c4 and c5 are shut. If the black king goes up, I go up with it: d5, d6. It stays locked on the a- and b-files, and once it is far enough, my pawn moves and my king goes after the black pawn. Ke5, which looks more active, doesn't win: only Kd4 wins.
step.d_wall: Follow the wall as it climbs, and the harvest at the end.
step.d_wall.m1: Kd4. The c-file is closed to the black king.
step.d_wall.m2: It tries to go up and around.
step.d_wall.m3: Kd5. I go up with it and the wall still stands.
step.d_wall.m5: Kd6. Now the black king is four files away from the f-pawn.
step.d_wall.m6: Kb7, and it still hasn't got through.
step.d_wall.m7: f4. Time for the pawn: the black king is too far away to interfere.
step.d_wall.m8: Kc8, still trying to reach d7 and e7.
step.d_wall.m9: Ke7. My king takes d8 away and gets close to f7.
step.d_wall.m10: The black pawn runs to f5.
step.d_wall.m13: Kxf5. Pawn won, king in front of my pawn and the black king far away. It's a win.
step.across: The longest case. The white king wants to go to the queenside and take the a-pawn, but if it runs now, the black king runs along and defends. So first my king walks down the f-file, next to the black king on the h-file, and pushes it to the bottom of the board. Only then do the pawn and the king go to the other side, with the black king too far away to catch up.
step.acrossMove: White to move and win. Push the black king down to the first rank, walking down beside it.
step.acrossMove.hint: Your king walks on the f-file, always on the same rank as the black king, to shut the g-file.
step.acrossMove.done: Perfect. The black king is in the bottom corner; now b3, Ke3, Kd4, Kc5 and the a-pawn falls.
step.t_away: White to move and win. The plan is to take the f7-pawn without losing yours. Kf5 looks like the natural way. Does it work?
step.t_away.hint1: After Kf5, where does the black king go? Is your f3-pawn left alone?
step.t_away.hint2: The black king wants to reach f3 via g2. Before going up, shut that door.
step.away: Kf5? Kg2, f4 and Kf3: the black king reaches my pawn and it's a draw. The right move is Kg3!, stepping away from f7. But from g3 my king shuts g2 and f2, and the black king is stuck on the first rank. Meanwhile the pawn climbs under protection. When it reaches f6, my king takes f7 and defends its own pawn at the same time.
step.d_away: Two shoulders in a row: one to keep the black king down, another to push it aside.
step.d_away.m1: Kg3. I shut g2 and f2. The black king can't come up.
step.d_away.m3: f4. The pawn moves, and my king looks after it.
step.d_away.m6: Ke2: the black king finally comes up, through the centre.
step.d_away.m7: Kf4! The second shoulder. I shut e3 and e4, and it has to go around.
step.d_away.m9: Ke5. I stay in front of it, on the way to d6.
step.d_away.m11: f6. Now Kd6 and Ke7, and the f7-pawn falls with my pawn protected.
step.awayMove: White to move and win. Repeat the plan: first keep the black king down, then the second shoulder.
step.awayMove.hint: The first move steps away from the f7-pawn and shuts g2.
step.awayMove.done: Right. Kg3 and then Kf4: the black king never got near the white pawn.
step.t_race: White to move. The black king is about to take f5 and get a passed pawn. Your a-pawn is far from it. Where should your king go?
step.t_race.hint1: After taking f5, the black king will come back to stop the a-pawn. Which way does it come?
step.t_race.hint2: Its route goes through d6, d7 and c8. Your king can get there first.
step.race: Kb5! The black king takes f5 and comes back: e6, d7, c8. My king goes to c6 and shuts d7 and d6. Notice that I protect nothing and attack nothing: I just stand in the way. The black king can't reach the a-pawn, so it runs with its own pawn. Both promote, but my queen is born first and checks on e8 and on f8, skewering the black queen.
step.d_race: Both pawns run. Count the tempi and watch the check at the end.
step.d_race.m2: Kxf5. The black king wins the pawn.
step.d_race.m3: a4. No time for another king move: the pawn has to go.
step.d_race.m4: Ke6, coming back for the a-pawn.
step.d_race.m5: Kc6! The shoulder: d6 and d7 are shut. The black king can't get through.
step.d_race.m6: With no way through, Black runs with the pawn.
step.d_race.m15: Qe8+! The black king on e6 is in check and can't go to d5, d6 or d7, which my king guards.
step.d_race.m17: Qf8+, and the queen on f1 is on the same file as the king.
step.d_race.m19: Qxf1. End of the race, and the king on c6 decided it.
step.raceMove: White to move and win. Your turn: king into the path, pawn at the right moment, and the shoulder.
step.raceMove.hint: The king heads for c6, where the black king will want to pass.
step.raceMove.done: Well done. With the king on c6, Black can't stop the a-pawn, and the race ends with your queen's two checks.
step.t_defend: White to move and draw. Taking f7 looks natural, but the b5-pawn is weak. What happens after Kf6, and which move holds?
step.t_defend.hint1: If your king goes to take f7, where does the black king go? It knows how to shoulder too.
step.t_defend.hint2: Think of the black king stuck on the h-file. Which square for your king shuts g4, g5 and g6 at once?
step.defend: Kf6? Kg4, Kxf7 Kf5! and the black king pushes mine: Ke7 Ke5, Kd7 Kd5, Kc7 Kc5, and the b5-pawn falls. Black uses the shoulder against me. That's why Kf5! I shut the g-file and the black king is stuck on the h-file. It goes down, I go down with it, and it never reaches my pawn. When Black runs out of ideas, my king goes after b6.
step.defendMove: White to move and draw. Keep the black king on the h-file and walk down with it.
step.defendMove.hint: Your king stays on the f-file, on the same rank as the black king.
step.defendMove.done: Right. The black king stayed stuck on the edge, and your b5-pawn was never in danger.
step.black: Now with Black, and to win. Kc5? to take a2 is slow: the white king gets back in time. Ke5! heads for the same place by another road, along the diagonal the white king needs. Kd4, Kc3, Kb2: each of my steps shuts its way, and the a2-pawn falls undefended.
step.blackMove: Black to move and win. Go and take the a2-pawn by the road that takes the white king out of play.
step.blackMove.hint: Walk along the diagonal the white king would use to come back, always one square ahead of it.
step.blackMove.done: Perfect. The white king stayed outside the whole time, and the a2-pawn is yours.
step.recap: Three rules. One: before running to a pawn, look where the other king wants to go; often the best move is to stand in its way. Two: the shoulder walks alongside, one rank or one file ahead, like a moving wall. Three: the right move may even step away from the target, like Kg3. The defender uses the same rules.
step.rulesMove: White to move and win. The black king wants to reach f5 and plant itself in front of the pawn. Don't let it.
step.rulesMove.hint: Shut f5 before it gets there.
step.rulesMove.done: Right. Kg4 and Kf4 keep the black king outside, and your king gets in front of the pawn.
step.last: To finish, a whole game. The black king wants to get back in front of the c-pawn. Your king is closer to its path than to the pawn: use that.
step.finish: White to move and win. Shoulder first, pawn later. I defend with Black.
ex.e02: White to move and win. The black king is in the corner. How does your king keep it there while the e-pawn runs?
ex.e02.hint: The black king would leave the corner via g8 and f8. One square shuts both.
ex.e02.solution: Kf7! shuts g8 and the black king's way back to the centre. It stays between h8, h7 and h6, and the e-pawn runs with nobody to stop it.
ex.e05: White to move and win. Your king wants to go and take the a4-pawn. Kf5 looks like the shortest way. Is it the best?
ex.e05.hint: The black king will run to c8, the good corner against a rook's pawn. Shut its road along the seventh rank.
ex.e05.solution: Kf6! (the only move) takes g7, f7 and e7 away from the black king. It has to go around along the eighth rank, and the white king reaches b6 first. With Kf5? the black king goes down via g7, f7, e7, reaches c8 and draws.
ex.e08: White to move and win. The plan is to take b7. Kc4 looks like the direct road. What is the right first move?
ex.e08.hint: Before heading for b7, keep the black king away from your a-pawn. It comes via f2 and e3.
ex.e08.solution: Ke2! (the only move) shuts f1, f2 and f3; then a4 and Ke3, also the only moves. The black king stays behind the white one all the way, and the white king reaches b7 without being caught. With Kc4? the black king comes via f2, e3, d4 and c4 and arrives in time.
ex.e10: Study by Grigoriev, 1932. White to move and win. The c7-pawn is about to run, and the black king wants to step into the square of your a-pawn. One move handles both.
ex.e10.hint: The black king heads for the queenside along the fourth rank. Shut that road and go for the c-pawn at the same time.
ex.e10.solution: Kf5!, Ke5! and Kd4!, all the only moves. The white king goes for the c-pawn and, at every step, shuts e4 and d4 to the black king. With a4? comes Ke4, and the black king is inside the pawn's square. In the end the white king takes the c-pawn and the black king arrives too late for the a-pawn.
ex.e11: Study by Duras, 1905. White to move and win. Your king has to stop the g-pawn and, at the same time, see the b-pawn home. Only one move does both.
ex.e11.hint: The black king will come back through the centre to catch your pawn. Put your king where it shuts that road without leaving the square of the g-pawn.
ex.e11.solution: Kc5! (the only move). The king stays inside the square of the g-pawn and already shuts d6 and d7 to the black king. After Kg6, b4, Kf7, b5, Ke7 comes Kc6, and the black king never gets in front of the pawn. With Kc4? Kg5 the black king returns via f6 and e7 in time; b3? only draws as well.
ex.e12: White to move and win. In a plain race both sides queen, and a c-pawn on the seventh with its king beside it draws against the queen. You need another plan.
ex.e12.hint: Before pushing the h-pawn, use your king to keep the black king out of that pawn's square, without blocking the diagonal of your future queen.
ex.e12.solution: Ke4! and Kd4!, both the only moves: the white king threatens the c-pawn and shoulders the black king away from the square of the h-pawn. Ke5? blocks the h8-b2 diagonal and draws; h4? at once is the race that draws. After Kb4 comes h4 and, against c5+, Ke3! (the only move), not d3, where it would take another check. At the end Kd2 watches c1: if the pawn queens, the king takes it; after Kb2, h8=Q comes with check.
ex.e13: Study by Mandler, 1938. White to move and win. Taking b7 or racing with the f-pawn look natural. Calculate first.
ex.e13.hint: The right move takes nothing and pushes nothing: it hands Black the first move in the race, but leaves your king on the road the black king needs.
ex.e13.solution: Kd6!! (the only move). If the b-pawn advances, the white king takes it further up and stands between the black king and the f-pawn. So Ka3, and Kc5! (the only move) stays in the way; the black king has to walk up the a-file to escort its pawn, and only then f4! (the only move) and the race belongs to White. With f4? b5 both sides queen and it's a draw; with Kxb7? Kb3 the black king catches the f-pawn; with Kb6? Kb3 it steps into the square.
key.stairs: The white king walks down beside the black one, like going down stairs, always taking the square it wanted, until it is left far from the pawn.
key.wall: The white king becomes a wall in the middle of the board: the black king cannot get across to the pawns.
key.across: Shouldering from one side of the board to the other: the white king keeps walking down between the black king and the far side, and never lets it cross.
key.away: Before going for the pawns, the white king takes one step sideways and blocks the black king's path, leaving it stranded far from everything.
key.race: Shouldering in a race: the white king advances and, with the same moves, keeps the black king out of the path of White's edge pawn.
key.defend: Shouldering also saves games: the white king stands in the black king's path and stops it helping its pawn. The exact square matters: one to the side, and you lose.
history: Shouldering means using your own king as a barrier: it stands in the enemy king's path and pushes it away without touching it, like a defender stepping into an attacker's path. It is one of the classic named ideas of pawn endings; Mark Dvoretsky gives it a section in his endgame manual, next to opposition and triangulation. It looks simple but it is very deceptive: several published studies and handouts give the wrong route, because a single square to one side is enough to turn a win into a loss. You have already met shouldering in passing in other lessons; here it is the main subject.
practice: Now a whole game of king and pawn against king. Before you move the pawn, put your king in the black king's way.
